# Number in serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1.0/struct.Number.html

`pub struct Number { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Represents a JSON number, whether integer or floating point.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Returns true if the `Number` is an integer between `i64::MIN` and
`i64::MAX`.

For any Number on which `is_i64` returns true, `as_i64` is guaranteed to
return the integer value.

Returns true if the `Number` is an integer between zero and `u64::MAX`.

For any Number on which `is_u64` returns true, `as_u64` is guaranteed to
return the integer value.

Returns true if the `Number` can be represented by f64.

For any Number on which `is_f64` returns true, `as_f64` is guaranteed to
return the floating point value.

Currently this function returns true if and only if both `is_i64` and
`is_u64` return false but this is not a guarantee in the future.

If the `Number` is an integer, represent it as i64 if possible. Returns
None otherwise.

If the `Number` is an integer, represent it as u64 if possible. Returns
None otherwise.

Represents the number as f64 if possible. Returns None otherwise.

Converts a finite `f64` to a `Number`. Infinite or NaN values are not JSON
numbers.

```
assert!(Number::from_f64(256.0).is_some());
assert!(Number::from_f64(f64::NAN).is_none());
```
If the `Number` is an integer, represent it as i128 if possible. Returns
None otherwise.

If the `Number` is an integer, represent it as u128 if possible. Returns
None otherwise.

A structure for serializing Rust values into JSON.

### impl<'a, W, F> [Serializer](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serializer.html) for &'a mut [Serializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Serializer.html)<W, F>

Serialize newtypes without an object wrapper.

The output type produced by this

`Serializer` during successful
serialization. Most serializers that produce text or binary output
should set `Ok = ()` and serialize into an [or buffer contained within the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html)`io::Write``Serializer` instance. Serializers that build
in-memory data structures may be simplified by using `Ok` to propagate
the data structure around.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_json/ser.rs.html#307-309)[§](https://docs.rs#method.serialize_tuple)#### fn [serialize_tuple](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serializer.html#tymethod.serialize_tuple)(self, len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeTuple](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeTuple)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_json/ser.rs.html#307-309)

# StreamDeserializer in serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1.0/struct.StreamDeserializer.html

`pub struct StreamDeserializer<'de, R, T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Iterator that deserializes a stream into multiple JSON values.

A stream deserializer can be created from any JSON deserializer using the
`Deserializer::into_iter` method.

The data can consist of any JSON value. Values need to be a self-delineating value e.g. arrays, objects, or strings, or be followed by whitespace or a self-delineating value.

```
use serde_json::{Deserializer, Value};
fn main() {
    let data = "{\"k\": 3}1\"cool\"\"stuff\" 3{}  [0, 1, 2]";
    let stream = Deserializer::from_str(data).into_iter::<Value>();
    for value in stream {
        println!("{}", value.unwrap());
    }
}
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_json/de.rs.html#2369-2442)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-StreamDeserializer%3C'de,+R,+T%3E)### impl<'de, R, T> [StreamDeserializer](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamDeserializer.html)<'de, R, T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_json/de.rs.html#2369-2442)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-StreamDeserializer%3C'de,+R,+T%3E)

### impl<'de, R, T> [StreamDeserializer](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamDeserializer.html)<'de, R, T>

Create a JSON stream deserializer from one of the possible serde_json input sources.

Typically it is more convenient to use one of these methods instead:

- Deserializer::from_str(…).into_iter()
- Deserializer::from_slice(…).into_iter()
- Deserializer::from_reader(…).into_iter()

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_json/de.rs.html#2424-2426)#### pub fn [byte_offset](https://docs.rs#method.byte_offset)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_json/de.rs.html#2424-2426)

#### pub fn [byte_offset](https://docs.rs#method.byte_offset)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)

Returns the number of bytes so far deserialized into a successful `T`.

If a stream deserializer returns an EOF error, new data can be joined to
`old_data[stream.byte_offset()..]` to try again.

```
let data = b"[0] [1] [";
let de = serde_json::Deserializer::from_slice(data);
let mut stream = de.into_iter::<Vec<i32>>();
assert_eq!(0, stream.byte_offset());
println!("{:?}", stream.next()); // [0]
assert_eq!(3, stream.byte_offset());
println!("{:?}", stream.next()); // [1]
assert_eq!(7, stream.byte_offset());
println!("{:?}", stream.next()); // error
assert_eq!(8, stream.byte_offset());
// If err.is_eof(), can join the remaining data to new data and continue.
let remaining = &data[stream.byte_offset()..];
```
*Note:* In the future this method may be changed to return the number of
bytes so far deserialized into a successful T *or* syntactically valid
JSON skipped over due to a type error. See [serde-rs/json#70](https://github.com/serde-rs/json/issues/70) for an
example illustrating this.

# from_value in serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1.0/fn.from_value.html

## Expand description

Interpret a `serde_json::Value` as an instance of type `T`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use serde::Deserialize;
use serde_json::json;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
struct User {
    fingerprint: String,
    location: String,
}
fn main() {
    // The type of `j` is `serde_json::Value`
    let j = json!({
        "fingerprint": "0xF9BA143B95FF6D82",
        "location": "Menlo Park, CA"
    });
    let u: User = serde_json::from_value(j).unwrap();
    println!("{:#?}", u);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

This conversion can fail if the structure of the Value does not match the
structure expected by `T`, for example if `T` is a struct type but the Value
contains something other than a JSON map. It can also fail if the structure
is correct but `T`’s implementation of `Deserialize` decides that something
is wrong with the data, for example required struct fields are missing from
the JSON map or some number is too big to fit in the expected primitive
type.

---

## Expand description

Serialize the given data structure as a pretty-printed String of JSON.

[§](#errors)Errors

Serialization can fail if `T`’s implementation of `Serialize` decides to
fail, or if `T` contains a map with non-string keys.

# to_value in serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1.0/fn.to_value.html

## Expand description

Convert a `T` into `serde_json::Value` which is an enum that can represent
any valid JSON data.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use serde::Serialize;
use serde_json::json;
use std::error::Error;
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct User {
    fingerprint: String,
    location: String,
}
fn compare_json_values() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let u = User {
        fingerprint: "0xF9BA143B95FF6D82".to_owned(),
        location: "Menlo Park, CA".to_owned(),
    };
    // The type of `expected` is `serde_json::Value`
    let expected = json!({
        "fingerprint": "0xF9BA143B95FF6D82",
        "location": "Menlo Park, CA",
    });
    let v = serde_json::to_value(u).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(v, expected);
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

This conversion can fail if `T`’s implementation of `Serialize` decides to
fail, or if `T` contains a map with non-string keys.

```
use std::collections::BTreeMap;
fn main() {
    // The keys in this map are vectors, not strings.
    let mut map = BTreeMap::new();
    map.insert(vec![32, 64], "x86");
    println!("{}", serde_json::to_value(map).unwrap_err());
}
```

---

# target_lexicon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/target-lexicon/latest/target-redirect/target_lexicon/index.html

## Expand description

LLVM target triple types.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [triple](https://docs.rs/macro.triple.html)
- A convenient syntax for triple literals.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultToHost.html)- ToHost
- A simple wrapper around `Triple`that provides an implementation of`Default`which defaults to`Triple::host()`.
- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultToUnknown.html)- ToUnknown
- A simple wrapper around `Triple`that provides an implementation of`Default`which defaults to`Triple::unknown()`.
- [Deployment](https://docs.rs/struct.DeploymentTarget.html)- Target
- The minimum OS version that we’re compiling for.
- [Triple](https://docs.rs/struct.Triple.html)
- An LLVM target “triple”. Historically such things had three fields, though they’ve added additional fields over time.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Aarch64](https://docs.rs/enum.Aarch64Architecture.html)- Architecture
- [Architecture](https://docs.rs/enum.Architecture.html)
- The “architecture” field, which in some cases also specifies a specific subarchitecture.
- [ArmArchitecture](https://docs.rs/enum.ArmArchitecture.html)
- [Binary](https://docs.rs/enum.BinaryFormat.html)- Format
- The “binary format” field, which is usually omitted, and the binary format is implied by the other fields.
- [CData](https://docs.rs/enum.CDataModel.html)- Model
- The C data model used on a target.
- [Calling](https://docs.rs/enum.CallingConvention.html)- Convention
- The calling convention, which specifies things like which registers are used for passing arguments, which registers are callee-saved, and so on.
- [Clever](https://docs.rs/enum.CleverArchitecture.html)- Architecture
- [Custom](https://docs.rs/enum.CustomVendor.html)- Vendor
- A string for a `Vendor::Custom`that can either be used in`const`contexts or hold dynamic strings.
- [Endianness](https://docs.rs/enum.Endianness.html)
- The target memory endianness.
- [Environment](https://docs.rs/enum.Environment.html)
- The “environment” field, which specifies an ABI environment on top of the operating system. In many configurations, this field is omitted, and the environment is implied by the operating system.
- [Mips32](https://docs.rs/enum.Mips32Architecture.html)- Architecture
- An enum for all 32-bit MIPS architectures (not just “MIPS32”).
- [Mips64](https://docs.rs/enum.Mips64Architecture.html)- Architecture
- An enum for all 64-bit MIPS architectures (not just “MIPS64”).
- [Operating](https://docs.rs/enum.OperatingSystem.html)- System
- The “operating system” field, which sometimes implies an environment, and sometimes isn’t an actual operating system.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)- Error
- An error returned from parsing a triple.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/enum.PointerWidth.html)- Width
- The width of a pointer (in the default address space).
- [Riscv32](https://docs.rs/enum.Riscv32Architecture.html)- Architecture
- An enum for all 32-bit RISC-V architectures.
- [Riscv64](https://docs.rs/enum.Riscv64Architecture.html)- Architecture
- An enum for all 64-bit RISC-V architectures.
- [Size](https://docs.rs/enum.Size.html)
- The size of a type.
- [Vendor](https://docs.rs/enum.Vendor.html)
- The “vendor” field, which in practice is little more than an arbitrary modifier.
- [X86_](https://docs.rs/enum.X86_32Architecture.html)- 32Architecture
- An enum for all 32-bit x86 architectures.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [HOST](https://docs.rs/constant.HOST.html)
- The `Triple`of the current host.

# triple in target_lexicon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/target-lexicon/latest/target-redirect/target_lexicon/macro.triple.html

```
macro_rules! triple {
    ($str:tt) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

A convenient syntax for triple literals.

This currently expands to code that just calls `Triple::from_str` and does
an `expect`, though in the future it would be cool to use procedural macros
or so to report errors at compile time instead.

---

# DeploymentTarget in target_lexicon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/target-lexicon/latest/target-redirect/target_lexicon/struct.DeploymentTarget.html

## Expand description

The minimum OS version that we’re compiling for.

This is formatted as `"major.minor.patch"`.

The size of the parts here are limited by Mach-O’s `LC_BUILD_VERSION`.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.major)

`major: `[u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u16.html)[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.minor)

`minor: `[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.patch)

# Triple in target_lexicon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/target-lexicon/latest/target-redirect/target_lexicon/struct.Triple.html

```
pub struct Triple {
    pub architecture:
```
[Architecture](https://docs.rs/enum.Architecture.html),
    pub vendor: [Vendor](https://docs.rs/enum.Vendor.html),
    pub operating_system: [OperatingSystem](https://docs.rs/enum.OperatingSystem.html),
    pub environment: [Environment](https://docs.rs/enum.Environment.html),
    pub binary_format: [BinaryFormat](https://docs.rs/enum.BinaryFormat.html),
}## Expand description

An LLVM target “triple”. Historically such things had three fields, though they’ve added additional fields over time.

Note that `Triple` doesn’t implement `Default` itself. If you want a type
which defaults to the host triple, or defaults to unknown-unknown-unknown,
use `DefaultToHost` or `DefaultToUnknown`, respectively.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.architecture)

`architecture: `[Architecture](https://docs.rs/enum.Architecture.html)The “architecture” (and sometimes the subarchitecture).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.vendor)

`vendor: `[Vendor](https://docs.rs/enum.Vendor.html)The “vendor” (whatever that means).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.operating_system)

`operating_system: `[OperatingSystem](https://docs.rs/enum.OperatingSystem.html)The “operating system” (sometimes also the environment).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.environment)

`environment: `[Environment](https://docs.rs/enum.Environment.html)The “environment” on top of the operating system (often omitted for operating systems with a single predominant environment).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.binary_format)

`binary_format: `[BinaryFormat](https://docs.rs/enum.BinaryFormat.html)The “binary format” (rarely used).

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# Aarch64Architecture in target_lexicon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/target-lexicon/latest/target-redirect/target_lexicon/enum.Aarch64Architecture.html

```
#[non_exhaustive]pub enum Aarch64Architecture {
    Aarch64,
    Aarch64be,
}
```
## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

Non-exhaustive enums could have additional variants added in future. Therefore, when matching against variants of non-exhaustive enums, an extra wildcard arm must be added to account for any future variants.

    LLP64,
    LP64,
    ILP64,
}
```
## Expand description

The C data model used on a target.

See also https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/language/arithmetic_types

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.LP32)

### LP32

The data model used most commonly on Win16. `long` and `pointer` are 32 bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ILP32)

### ILP32

The data model used most commonly on Win32 and 32-bit Unix systems.

`int`, `long`, and `pointer` are all 32 bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.LLP64)

### LLP64

The data model used most commonly on Win64

`long long`, and `pointer` are 64 bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.LP64)

### LP64

The data model used most commonly on 64-bit Unix systems

`long`, and `pointer` are 64 bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ILP64)

### ILP64

A rare data model used on early 64-bit Unix systems

`int`, `long`, and `pointer` are all 64 bits.

# CallingConvention in target_lexicon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/target-lexicon/latest/target-redirect/target_lexicon/enum.CallingConvention.html

```
#[non_exhaustive]pub enum CallingConvention {
    SystemV,
    WasmBasicCAbi,
    WindowsFastcall,
    AppleAarch64,
}
```
## Expand description

The calling convention, which specifies things like which registers are used for passing arguments, which registers are callee-saved, and so on.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SystemV)

### SystemV

“System V”, which is used on most Unix-like platfoms. Note that the specific conventions vary between hardware architectures; for example, x86-32’s “System V” is entirely different from x86-64’s “System V”.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.WasmBasicCAbi)

### WasmBasicCAbi

The WebAssembly C ABI. https://github.com/WebAssembly/tool-conventions/blob/master/BasicCABI.md

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.WindowsFastcall)

### WindowsFastcall

“Windows Fastcall”, which is used on Windows. Note that like “System V”, this varies between hardware architectures. On x86-32 it describes what Windows documentation calls “fastcall”, and on x86-64 it describes what Windows documentation often just calls the Windows x64 calling convention (though the compiler still recognizes “fastcall” as an alias for it).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AppleAarch64)

### AppleAarch64

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

A string for a `Vendor::Custom` that can either be used in `const`
contexts or hold dynamic strings.

An owned `String`. This supports the general case.

### Static(&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.str.html))

A static `str`, so that `CustomVendor` can be constructed in `const`
contexts.

### Darwin([Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[DeploymentTarget](https://docs.rs/struct.DeploymentTarget.html)>)

The general [Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darwin_(operating_system)) core OS.

Generally, `-mmacosx-version-min=...` or similar flags are required by
Clang to determine the actual OS (either macOS, iOS, tvOS, watchOS or
visionOS).

WARNING: When parsing `rustc` target triples, this matches the macOS
target triples as well.
